prompt:
Below are claims about one researcher (TARGET), extracted from their writing, and a sample of claims about four other researchers in the same field (PEERS).

Write 8 statements of how TARGET differs from PEERS on how to design, run and interpret evaluations and alignment experiments. Each starts "Unlike peers, ...". Leave out anything PEERS also hold. At most 250 words in total. Do not name any person, organisation, paper or model. Output only the 8 statements, one per line, each starting "- Unlike peers, ".

TARGET:

- (D5) Attributes surface regularities in generated data to the framing of the generation protocol and to the heuristics people adopt to produce items quickly, so the setup itself leaves detectable fingerprints.
- (D2) In a setup, avoid copying a single canonical example or template into the instructions to the generator instead of varying demonstrations, because it primes stereotyped patterns that become tells.
- (D2) Distrusts human-written data because writing introduces artifacts that models exploit via spurious statistical patterns, so a benchmark's apparent performance may not reflect the intended capability.
- (D3) Prefers benchmarks whose scores validly reflect the target capability over benchmarks that are merely hard for current models, because difficulty by adversarial selection does not show that a result reflects the intended behavior.
- (D3) Distrusts evaluation data containing annotation artifacts, since a system can reach strong scores by shortcuts rather than by the intended behaviors; test setups should not be solvable or triggerable by superficial cues.
- (D2) Prefers naturally-occurring distributions over hand-built ones where viable because they reduce the risk that the benchmark is skewed in ways that omit important phenomena, though acknowledges they are often not viable.
- (D2) Distrusts expert-authored test data for broad benchmarks because designers' knowledge of what matters steers examples toward known phenomena, which is relevant to auditor-written scenarios that reflect the designer's expectations about what is being tested.
- (D3) Prefers evaluation sets that still accurately reflect the target capability over sets that are merely harder, because narrow optimization against a particular model stops measuring the intended ability.
- (D3) Prefers evaluating across a wide range of models over measuring difficulty with the adversary model itself, because the adversary is disproportionately affected and difficulty is overstated.

- (D3) Prefers setups where the proxy participants are genuinely misaligned over setups that differ only in capability, because with a pure capability gap the optimal behavior is trivial and the result teaches little.
- (D3) Distrusts results from proxy setups as stand-ins for real settings, since current models are misaligned in different ways than transformative ones and many apparent failures are really capability gaps.

PEERS:
- In a setup, distort real observations so they resemble the synthetic ones (as well as improving the synthetic ones), because shrinking the distinguishability gap from both sides makes eval-vs-deployment detection harder.
- In a setup, use an in-world, plausible cue (free-tier vs paid-tier user) to signal training vs unmonitored instead of an explicit 'you are being tested/trained' statement, because it seems realistic and avoids confounds about the model reacting to whether it is talking to a real user.
- Prefers realism in the safety-training/evaluation pipeline over realism in how the misaligned behavior was instilled, because the question under test is whether the defenses work, not whether the threat arises naturally.
- Rejects an understanding standard that is satisfied trivially or tied to one method, e.g. causal scrubbing only guarantees sufficiency, not necessity, of an explanation.
- prefers red teams that search for the best attack strategies over ones that imitate what an evil AI would psychologically plan, because security-style adversarial analysis should not rely on guessing the attacker's psychology.
- Prefers testing safety against a red-team attack policy that actively exploits the protocol's weaknesses over testing with the honest model's behavior, because safety must hold even when the model is intentionally subverting.
- Distrusts evaluation results where the protocol/blue team can tell eval from deployment, because it can behave differently (cheat) when it detects which is being measured.
- Treats introspection as a risk because models with privileged self-knowledge could infer facts about how they are evaluated and gaming those evaluations, which bears directly on eval-awareness.
- Construct analogous test settings by finding a similar setting where you have strictly more information (sandwiching, backtesting) and restricting the overseer to the information available in the real setting of interest.
- Treats evidence of research competence as concrete artifacts (papers, blog posts, courses, reference letters) rather than formal credentials, a preference for demonstrable output over credentials.
- Prefers worst-case (a single failure counts) safety metrics over average performance because rare catastrophic actions are what matter.
- Accepts a model organism as valid when the dangerous behavior is causally downstream of the reasoning step of interest (verified by editing the chain of thought), even if the model was seeded via instruction-following, but flags this as weaker for interpretability claims.
- Prefers proxy bad outcomes that are benign but share the core difficulty (capture-the-flag style) over real catastrophic objectives, because they are safe to run and cleanly checkable.
- Test behavior under monitored vs. unmonitored cues in the environment (e.g. reward function overwriting only when apparently unobserved) to reveal conditional misbehavior.
- Chooses to test generalization from easily discoverable misbehavior to rarer, more serious misbehavior, since sophisticated behavior may be too hard to find by exploration alone.
- In a setup, write the system prompt to read like plausible operator instructions and give no explicit goal or mention of the target behavior, instead of instructing or hinting at it, because the behavior should emerge from the model's own preferences.
- prefers humans who know the AI well hand-crafting tempting inputs for adversarial training over relying on any single method, because it is one useful technique in a smorgasbord but not a full solution against deception.
- Prefers staying focused on the core catastrophic risks over an 'Everything-Bagel' approach that tries to cover every possible harm, because a scattered agenda becomes unviable.
- Prefers not to over-update on null results because the target behavior is adversarially hidden by the model, so failing to elicit it is weak evidence of absence.
- Prefers evaluations built on easy-to-measure capability assumptions over ones that depend on hard-to-test properties, because the latter let developers make flawed or cherry-picked safety arguments from weak, illegible evidence.
- prefers an empirical per-domain measurement over intuition about whether checking is easier than generating, because answers depend on the specific domain and can be directly evaluated.
- Prefers causal intervention on the model's reasoning (editing the chain-of-thought) over inspecting plausible-looking reasoning samples, because samples alone could be regurgitated training data.

- prefers safety evidence that goes beyond surface-level behavioral testing because AIs can appear well-behaved while harboring secret motives.
- Spend most effort on conservative-assumption evaluations, then upweight techniques that only work if assumptions fail in an ad hoc way, because classic control evals systematically undervalue such techniques.
- In a setup, resolve model strategies by placing an actual model instance in a mock-up of the realistic situation (e.g., running interpretability experiments) instead of just judging abstract plans or merely causing failures, because only realistic deception of overseers counts as success.

result:
- Unlike peers, TARGET tests whether a benchmark can be solved by a hypothesis-only or ablated baseline that never sees the intended signal, and treats high scores without that check as likely shortcut learning.
- Unlike peers, TARGET splits evaluation data into artifact-solvable and artifact-resistant subsets and treats the gap between them as a measure of how much success rests on surface cues.
- Unlike peers, TARGET prefers balancing artifacts across labels to filtering out artifact-bearing examples, because filtering creates new artifacts and removes real phenomena.
- Unlike peers, TARGET treats both human-written and LLM-generated data as bias sources, and mitigates them by varying worker prompts and avoiding a single canonical template in generator instructions.
- Unlike peers, TARGET checks adversarially built sets for self-targeting bias by comparing item rankings with and without the evaluated model as the adversary, and expects zero rank change for a fair set.
- Unlike peers, TARGET distrusts simple accuracy on contentious items, because collapsing a distribution of human labels to one label makes scores misleading, and scores against the full label distribution instead.
- Unlike peers, TARGET tests a new protocol first with idealized, skilled human participants in an oracle setting before using current language models, treating that as the cleaner test of whether the direction is viable.
- Unlike peers, TARGET treats consistency across many models and settings as the main evidence of a systematic cause, and declines to draw conclusions from tiny evaluation sets.
